tree-parts-mixup.label: Mixing up the parts of a tree
tree-parts-mixup.feedback: Check the definitions: a leaf has no children, a child is one link below its parent, and a subtree is a node plus everything below it.

rule-reversed.label: Reversing the BST rule
rule-reversed.feedback: Smaller values go left and larger values go right. Picture the root of a sorted class list: earlier names to the left, later names to the right.

any-binary-tree.label: Thinking any binary tree is a BST
any-binary-tree.feedback: Having at most two children only makes a tree binary. Look for a value deeper in the left subtree that is larger than the root: that one value breaks the BST rule.

local-check-only.label: Only checking a node against its direct children
local-check-only.feedback: The rule covers the whole subtree. A node can sit correctly next to its parent and still be on the wrong side of a node higher up.

shape-not-order.label: Thinking the BST rule is about shape
shape-not-order.feedback: A BST node can have zero, one or two children. The rule is only about the order of the values, not how many children a node has.

search-checks-every-node.label: Thinking search checks every node
search-checks-every-node.feedback: Search follows one path from the root. Each comparison sends it left or right, so the other branch is never looked at.

wrong-child-or-skips.label: Following the wrong child or skipping a node
wrong-child-or-skips.feedback: Compare at every node on the way down. Smaller means go left, larger means go right, and no level can be skipped.

not-found-confusion.label: Stopping at the closest value
not-found-confusion.feedback: Search only reports found when a node equals the key. Reaching an empty link means the value is not in the tree, however close the last node was.

insert-moves-nodes.label: Thinking an insert moves existing nodes
insert-moves-nodes.feedback: An insert follows the search path to an empty link and adds a new leaf there. Existing nodes never move, and the newest value never becomes the root.

traversal-order-mixup.label: Mixing up the traversal orders
traversal-order-mixup.feedback: Pre-order visits the node before its subtrees, in-order between them and post-order after them. Replay the traversal and watch when each node is visited, not when it is first reached.

inorder-always-sorted.label: Thinking in-order is sorted for any tree
inorder-always-sorted.feedback: In-order gives sorted output only because of the BST rule. On a binary tree that breaks the rule, in-order output is not sorted.

always-balanced.label: Thinking a BST is always balanced
always-balanced.feedback: The insert order decides the shape. Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the tree becomes a chain, so a search can need up to n comparisons instead of about log n.

cost-not-height.label: Not linking search cost to height
cost-not-height.feedback: Each comparison moves down one level, so the most comparisons a search needs equals the height of the tree.

array-insert-cost.label: Forgetting the cost of inserting into a sorted array
array-insert-cost.feedback: Adding to a sorted array means shifting later items to keep the order. Appending at the end breaks the order that binary search depends on.

bst-always-better.label: Thinking a BST is always the better choice
bst-always-better.feedback: Match the structure to the workload. If the data never changes and arrives sorted, a sorted array with binary search avoids the chain-shaped BST problem.
